set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters
set1.q: What kind of specimen does reagent strip testing require?
opts: A first-morning specimen only
A fresh specimen is required; it need not be the first of the day.
Any specimen collected within the past day
A specimen brought in from the day before is no longer fresh.
A specimen collected after a preservative is added
No preservative is added.
A fresh specimen in a sterile container
Correct — both the freshness and the sterile container matter.

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters
set1.q: What happens to the fluid and waste that the tubules do not reabsorb?
opts: It is stored in the renal cortex
The cortex does not store filtrate.
It returns to the glomerulus to be filtered again
Filtrate moves forward through the nephron rather than back.
It becomes urine
Correct — whatever is not reabsorbed is excreted as urine.
It is broken down by tubular enzymes
The tubules reabsorb rather than digest the filtrate.
set1.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 15

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters
set1.q: Which additional elements does a microscopic urinalysis report?
opts: Red cells, white cells, epithelial cells, casts, and crystals
Correct — those are the sediment findings.
Only bacteria and yeast
Organisms are part of it, but the sediment carries more.
Only casts and crystals
Cells are reported as well.
The same nine analytes as the dipstick, measured precisely
Microscopy reports different elements rather than remeasuring the pads.
set1.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 33

set1.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations
set1.q: A patient has heavy protein on the dipstick and foamy urine. Which finding on inspection matched the pad?
opts: The colour
Colour points to concentration, bilirubin, or blood.
The foam
Correct — foaming is associated with protein.
The odour
Odour points to infection or ketones.
The transparency
Turbidity points to cells, organisms, or crystals.
set1.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 8

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters
set1.q: What does ketonuria indicate about how cells are producing energy?
opts: They have stopped producing energy altogether
Ketones mark a change of fuel rather than a halt.
They are metabolising glucose instead of fatty acids
That is the normal state and produces no ketones.
They are metabolising protein instead of carbohydrate
Protein breakdown is not what produces ketones.
They are metabolising fatty acids instead of glucose
Correct — ketones are the by-product of that switch.
set1.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: b — Differentiate between hematuria, hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria
set1.q: Where does the myoglobin in myoglobinuria come from?
opts: Damaged skeletal muscle
Correct — muscle injury releases it.
Destroyed circulating red cells
Those release hemoglobin.
Bleeding from the bladder wall
That gives intact red cells.
The liver, after conjugation
The liver conjugates bilirubin, not myoglobin.
set1.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 26

set1.io: b — Differentiate between hematuria, hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria
set1.q: A healthy patient has a trace of blood on the dipstick after a hard run. How is that read?

Hemolysis would not be assumed from a trace after exercise.

A stone is one cause among several, not the only reading.
A trace can follow strenuous exercise
Correct — exercise can produce a small amount.
It indicates the specimen was contaminated
Exercise is the simpler explanation.

set1.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations
set1.q: A 28-year-old woman has two days of dysuria, frequency, and urgency with mild suprapubic tenderness. She is afebrile with no flank pain. What is the next step?
opts: Renal ultrasound
Imaging is not the first move in an uncomplicated lower tract presentation.
Urinalysis
Correct — it is quick, non-invasive, and answers the question in front of you.
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis

Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen alone

Dehydration
Dehydration concentrates the urine without spilling glucose.
A urinary tract infection with Escherichia coli
Infection does not itself spill glucose.
Renal disease that impairs tubular reabsorption
Correct — the leak is tubular rather than a high blood level.

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters

Excreting bicarbonate and reabsorbing hydrogen ions
That reverses both halves.
Excreting hydrogen ions and keeping bicarbonate
Correct — acid out, bicarbonate kept and made.
Excreting urea and reabsorbing creatinine
Neither is a route for acid-base control.

set1.io: b — Differentiate between hematuria, hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters

set1.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations
set1.q: A patient passes large volumes of very dilute urine with a low specific gravity. Which condition fits?
opts: Heart failure
Reduced renal blood flow concentrates the urine.
The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone

Dehydration

Diabetes insipidus

set1.q: Which of these lowers the specific gravity through the kidney's own failure to concentrate?
opts: Chronic kidney disease

Heart failure

Hypotension

Renal artery stenosis

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters

Make the urine more alkaline
Correct — alkalinising the urine is the management for uric acid stones.

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters

opts: White cells release them as they degranulate

Bacteria reduce urinary nitrates to nitrites
Correct — bacterial reductase performs the conversion.
The renal tubules secrete them when acidotic

They are filtered unchanged from the plasma
They are generated in the urine by bacteria.

set1.io: b — Differentiate between hematuria, hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria
set1.q: The blood pad is positive, microscopy shows no red cells, and the serum creatine phosphokinase is raised. Which is it?
opts: Myoglobinuria
Correct — a raised creatine phosphokinase points to muscle.
Hemoglobinuria
That would raise the unconjugated bilirubin instead.
Hematuria
Intact cells would be visible.
Contamination of the specimen
Contamination does not raise the creatine phosphokinase.

set1.io: b — Differentiate between hematuria, hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria

set1.io: b — Differentiate between hematuria, hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria
set1.q: How is gross hematuria distinguished from microscopic hematuria?
opts: Gross is visible to the naked eye; microscopic needs analysis to detect
Correct — visibility is the distinction.
Gross comes from the kidney; microscopic comes from the bladder
Either can arise anywhere along the tract.

Gross means more than three red cells; microscopic means fewer

set1.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations
set1.q: A patient with recurrent stones has persistently alkaline urine and repeated infections. Which stone type does that combination suggest?
opts: Uric acid
Those form in acidic urine.
Struvite
Correct — alkaline urine with urease-producing organisms.
Calcium oxalate
Those are associated with acidic urine.
Cystine
Not the type this combination points to.
set1.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters

Correct — contamination is the recognised false positive.
Refrigeration of the specimen

A high fluid intake before collection

Reading the pad after ten minutes
Late reading is an error but not the recognised false positive here.
set1.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 28

set1.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations

opts: Treat empirically for cystitis

Correct — squamous cells and no symptoms point to contamination.

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters

opts: Only the microscopic sediment, after centrifugation

Only the chemical contents, read from a reagent strip

Correct — all three together make up the test.

set1.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations
set1.q: A patient is found after several hours trapped under a fallen beam. The dipstick is positive for blood but no red cells are seen. Which test confirms the source?

Correct — a raised level points to muscle as the source.

set1.io: b — Differentiate between hematuria, hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria
set1.q: Which of these is a recognised cause of hemoglobinuria?
opts: Over-aggressive anticoagulation
That produces bleeding and intact red cells.
Statin therapy

Correct — extensive burns destroy red cells intravascularly.
Electric shock
That damages muscle, giving myoglobinuria.
set1.cite: 6. Urinalysis Diagnostics SV Gopal Fall 2026.pptx, Slide 25

set1.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters
set1.q: More than twenty squamous epithelial cells per high power field are seen. How should the specimen be read?
opts: It is likely contaminated
Correct — that many squamous cells points to contamination.

set1.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations

That gives pyuria and nitrites rather than glucose and ketones.
Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
Correct — glucose spilling with ketones from fatty acid metabolism.
Rhabdomyolysis
That gives a positive blood pad with a raised creatine phosphokinase.
Biliary obstruction
That gives bilirubin in the urine.

set2.io: c — Correlate urinalysis findings with common clinical presentations

opts: Heme

set2.io: a — Describe the following urinalysis parameters

The patient is in ketoacidosis

set2.q: A toddler is being assessed for a urinary tract infection and the nitrite pad is negative. What limits that result here?
opts: Children void too often for the conversion
Correct — the conversion needs urine to sit in the bladder.
The pad cannot be used under the age of five
It can be used; the interval between voids is the limitation.
Children produce no urinary nitrates
Nitrates are present; the time to convert them is what is short.
Paediatric specimens must be refrigerated first
Refrigeration is not the issue here.

set2.q: Persistent proteinuria is best understood as what?
opts: Proof of nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome sits at the massive end rather than being proven by any protein.
A normal variant in most adults
Only a transient trace is normal, not persistent protein.
A significant sign of renal disease
Correct — persistence is what makes it significant.
Evidence of urinary tract infection
Infection shows on other pads.

set2.q: Why does a negative nitrite result fail to exclude a urinary tract infection?

Temperature is not the limitation.

Refrigeration is not what limits this pad.
Escherichia coli is rarely urease-positive
Correct — the commonest organism does not turn the pad positive.

set2.q: In a patient with cystitis, which negative dipstick results help to rule other things out?
opts: Glucose, ketones, bilirubin, and protein
Correct — their absence points away from metabolic, hepatic, and glomerular causes.
Specific gravity, pH, and appearance
Both always carry a value rather than being negative.
Leukocyte esterase and nitrites
Those are the positives that support the diagnosis.
Blood and leukocyte esterase
Both are positive in this picture.
